title: Fan Li Leaves at the Peak
text:
Fan Li was one of the two chief ministers who helped King Gou Jian of Yue recover from defeat and finally destroy the rival state of Wu in 473 BC. At the moment of triumph he was among the most honored men in the kingdom.

Sima Qian says that Fan Li then decided to leave. He judged that great fame makes a man hard to keep safe, and that Gou Jian was a ruler with whom one could share hardship but not good fortune. He departed by boat with his family and possessions. From abroad he wrote to his colleague Wen Zhong a warning that became proverbial: when the birds are all shot, the good bow is put away; when the cunning hare is dead, the hunting dog is cooked. He urged Wen Zhong to leave too.

Wen Zhong stayed, though he began to stay away from court claiming illness. Before long he was accused of plotting rebellion, and Gou Jian sent him a sword, the signal to kill himself, which he did.

Fan Li, meanwhile, settled in Qi under another name, farmed and traded, and grew rich. Later he moved to Tao, a busy trading center, and as Tao Zhu Gong became so famous for his wealth that his name was a byword for a successful merchant. Sima Qian adds that he gave much of his fortune away and made it again.
lesson: Knowing when to step away is part of strategy. Read the people you serve, and do not assume that what you were valued for in a struggle will protect you after it.
people: Fan Li, Wen Zhong, Gou Jian of Yue
location: Yue (modern Zhejiang), Qi and Tao (modern Shandong), China
source: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), chapters 41 and 129
